bottleneck: Sleep occupies a third of human life and its disruption damages every organ system, yet why the brain needs to go offline remains disputed. Competing accounts — memory consolidation, metabolic waste clearance via the glymphatic system, synaptic homeostasis, emotional processing — each have supporting evidence, but no unified theory explains why all of them require unconsciousness rather than quiet wakefulness. Without knowing sleep's core function, treating insomnia is symptomatic tinkering, and the links between poor sleep and Alzheimer's, depression, and metabolic disease cannot be mechanistically addressed.
current_state: The glymphatic clearance hypothesis gained support from animal work, but human evidence remains indirect. Sleep's fundamental purpose is still actively debated with no consensus in sight.

title: Sleep's core function still disputed
why_it_blocks: A third of human life serves a purpose science cannot name. Defining it would reframe everything from Alzheimer's prevention to mental health treatment — and the current answer is a list of candidates, not an explanation.
